My name is Blake Hunter Yagman, I am the managing attorney and principal of YAGMAN PLLC - a plaintiffs litigation boutique which challenges corporate malfeasance in courtrooms across the country.

My firm filed the first ever surveillance pricing case against JetBlue Airways, as well as the first ever surveillance wage fixing case against Uber. I was also responsible for helping to prepare the Senate Judiciary Committee for its investigatory hearing on dynamic and surveillance pricing.

For years, companies have weaponized consumer data against their own consumers. This started with the differentiation of pricing in catalogues and persisted, becoming more advanced, into the digital age. The harms are two-fold: (1) different pricing and price discrimination for individuals seeking to purchase the same goods and services or looking to perform the same type of labor and (2) the privacy related harms associated with the mass surveillance and surreptitious data collection needed to power the surveillance pricing apparatus.

It is imperative that we protect both consumer and labor rights, as well as privacy rights, which are fundamental legal cornerstones in an age where the use and sale of personal data is the secondary practice of every corporation. The Federal Trade Commission has an obligation to ensure that Section 5 of the FTC Act protects the rights of Americans vulnerable to data that they generally never know is being collected.

Respectfully Submitted,

Blake Hunter Yagman

COMMENT OF SIRVEIL, INC. - Docket FTC-2026-1057, Matter No. P034101. Full comment attached.

Disclosure of interest, first. I run Sirveil, Inc., a two-person California company. We operate a service that answers one narrow question: for a named individual and a named website, is that individual's information indexed on that site right now, returning the source URL, the matching text, and the time of retrieval. We do not remove data and we do not sell data about people. I have a commercial interest in the subject of this comment and disclose it here, as I do when I give public comment on the record at the California Privacy Protection Agency. Nothing I recommend below requires anyone to buy anything from my company, and I have written the recommendation so it could be satisfied by any competent independent party, including the Commission's own staff.

THE GAP: the Commission proposes to police a fact it currently has no independent way to establish.

The proposed statement reaches the undisclosed collection or use of personal data to set an individual's price. That is the right thing to reach, and the hardest thing in the statement to prove. To establish that a seller used personal data to price a consumer, the Commission must establish what data the seller held, and today that is established either by the seller's own attestation or by discovery into the seller's own systems. Both are inward-looking. Both depend on records maintained by the party whose conduct is at issue.

There is a third source of evidence, currently unused: much of the personal data that prices consumers is purchased, and the sellers of it are publicly observable. A consumer record offered by a data broker can be observed from the outside, by anyone, at a specific moment, and preserved with its source and timestamp. That evidence does not depend on the respondent's cooperation and does not require discovery.

WHY THIS MATTERS MOST AT THE REMEDY STAGE.

When the Commission resolves a matter involving improperly collected or used personal data, the order commonly requires deletion. Compliance is then measured by the respondent's own compliance report. That is a closed loop: the party that must delete the data reports whether the data was deleted, using systems only it can see.

The gap has a specific mechanism. Personal data sold onward does not have a single location. A seller can delete its own copy in complete good faith and be entirely accurate in its compliance report, while the same records remain publicly indexed at the brokers it bought from, available to re-acquire tomorrow. A deletion remedy verified only inside the respondent can be fully satisfied while the consumer's exposure is unchanged. From the consumer's position, nothing happened.

RECOMMENDATION.

I recommend the Commission add language to the policy statement, or carry the principle into orders under it, to the following effect:

"Where an enforcement action concerns the collection or use of personal data obtained from third parties, compliance with any deletion or data-disposition requirement should be demonstrable by at least one evidentiary stream that does not originate from the respondent, including, where the data was obtained from a publicly accessible source, dated observation of whether the individual's information remains available at that source."

Three notes on what that language is not doing.

It does not require a particular technology or vendor. Dated observation of a public source can be performed by a Commission investigator, a court-appointed monitor, a state attorney general, an academic researcher or a compliance auditor. My company sells an instrument for it; the recommendation stands without us and I would rather it were adopted in a form that has nothing to do with us.

It does not ask for certainty the evidence cannot support. Observation of a public source establishes what was publicly available at a moment, from a named source, and nothing more. It cannot establish what is inside a respondent's systems and should never be characterised as doing so. It is most useful precisely because it is the one input the respondent does not produce.

It is honest about ambiguity. A name alone frequently cannot distinguish one person from another. Any evidentiary standard should require an indeterminate result to be reported as indeterminate. A regime that pressures its participants toward clean negatives will produce clean negatives, and they will be worth nothing.

A NARROWER DRAFTING POINT. I would encourage the Commission not to limit the disclosure analysis to the price itself. For a consumer, "this price was set using data about you" and "this price was set using data you asked to have deleted last year" are materially different, and the second produces the injury the Commission is responding to. Whether that occurred is checkable today, from the outside.

Respectfully submitted, Ben Tobin, Founder and CEO, Sirveil, Inc., San Jose, California.

comment:
The FTC is on solid ground when it insists that sellers tell the truth about prices. It should not,
however, transform that principle into a general duty to disclose the mechanics of price formation
whenever the Commission believes consumers expect uniform pricing. Established Section 5 deception doctrine requires a deceptive representation, omission, or practice—not simply a consumer preconception. Section 5(n) unfairness doctrine requires proof of net consumer injury after accounting
for competitive benefits. A final statement built around those limits, coupled with express protection for individualized discounts, would deter genuine deception and unfairness while preserving price competition and experimentation that can lower prices and expand output.

comment:
Re: FTC-2026-1057 — Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing

I am the founder and CEO of Papercraft Miracles LLC, a woman-owned small manufacturing and creative business based in Buffalo, New York. Since 2013, we have manufactured handmade paper products, stationery, books, paper flowers, plantable seed products, event décor, wedding products and custom corporate gifts for consumers, retailers and corporate clients.

I support the FTC's goal of protecting consumers from undisclosed personalized pricing based on personal data. Consumers should not unknowingly be charged more for the same product because a company has used browsing history, purchasing behavior, location, income estimates or other personal information to determine that they may be willing to pay more.

However, I encourage the Commission to clearly distinguish this practice from legitimate customized and negotiated pricing, particularly for small businesses and custom manufacturers.

For a business like mine, two customers may receive different prices for seemingly similar products because of quantity, materials, customization, labor, production method, packaging, turnaround time, shipping, wholesale versus retail quantities, design requirements or overall project scope. These differences have nothing to do with the customer's perceived willingness or ability to pay.

For example, two customers may each request 100 wedding invitations, but one order may require custom handmade paper containing the customer's flowers, specialty printing, hand-torn edges, custom artwork and additional assembly. The other may use standard materials and require significantly less production time. Their prices will be different because the products and production costs are different—not because of who the customers are.

The same applies to business-to-business transactions. We manufacture custom corporate gifts and quote projects based on quantity, production requirements, customization, packaging, deadlines and other specifications. We also offer volume and wholesale pricing and may negotiate terms for large contracts.

I encourage the FTC to explicitly clarify that personalized pricing does not include price differences reasonably based on objective characteristics of the product, service or transaction rather than personal data used to estimate a customer's willingness to pay.

This should include legitimate practices such as custom quotes based on materials, labor and production requirements; quantity and volume discounts; wholesale pricing; negotiated B2B contracts; pricing based on turnaround, shipping or fulfillment requirements; customization and project complexity; and transparent promotional, group or loyalty discounts.

Clear guidance would protect consumers while preventing unnecessary uncertainty and compliance burdens for small businesses. A small manufacturer should not have to wonder whether giving two customers different custom quotes could be considered "personalized pricing" simply because the resulting prices differ.

At the same time, small businesses should be held to the same basic standard of transparency when personal consumer information is actually used to determine what an individual is likely willing to pay. If a business uses information about the person rather than the transaction to secretly increase that person's price, consumers deserve to know.

I therefore support the FTC's effort while asking the Commission to establish a clear distinction between who the customer is and what the customer is purchasing.

If a price varies because of who the customer is, based on personal data and estimated willingness to pay, transparency protections are appropriate. If it varies because the product, quantity, materials, labor, production requirements or contractual terms differ, it should be clearly recognized as ordinary customized pricing rather than personalized pricing.

Janna Willoughby-Lohr
Founder & CEO
Papercraft Miracles LLC
Buffalo, New York

comment_text:
Re: FTC-2026-1057 — Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing

I am the founder and CEO of Papercraft Miracles LLC, a woman-owned small manufacturing and creative business based in Buffalo, New York. Since 2013, we have manufactured handmade paper products, stationery, books, paper flowers, plantable seed products, event décor, wedding products and custom corporate gifts for consumers, retailers and corporate clients.

I support the FTC's goal of protecting consumers from undisclosed personalized pricing based on personal data. Consumers should not unknowingly be charged more for the same product because a company has used browsing history, purchasing behavior, location, income estimates or other personal information to determine that they may be willing to pay more.

However, I encourage the Commission to clearly distinguish this practice from legitimate customized and negotiated pricing, particularly for small businesses and custom manufacturers.

For a business like mine, two customers may receive different prices for seemingly similar products because of quantity, materials, customization, labor, production method, packaging, turnaround time, shipping, wholesale versus retail quantities, design requirements or overall project scope. These differences have nothing to do with the customer's perceived willingness or ability to pay.

For example, two customers may each request 100 wedding invitations, but one order may require custom handmade paper containing the customer's flowers, specialty printing, hand-torn edges, custom artwork and additional assembly. The other may use standard materials and require significantly less production time. Their prices will be different because the products and production costs are different—not because of who the customers are.

The same applies to business-to-business transactions. We manufacture custom corporate gifts and quote projects based on quantity, production requirements, customization, packaging, deadlines and other specifications. We also offer volume and wholesale pricing and may negotiate terms for large contracts.

I encourage the FTC to explicitly clarify that personalized pricing does not include price differences reasonably based on objective characteristics of the product, service or transaction rather than personal data used to estimate a customer's willingness to pay.

This should include legitimate practices such as custom quotes based on materials, labor and production requirements; quantity and volume discounts; wholesale pricing; negotiated B2B contracts; pricing based on turnaround, shipping or fulfillment requirements; customization and project complexity; and transparent promotional, group or loyalty discounts.

Clear guidance would protect consumers while preventing unnecessary uncertainty and compliance burdens for small businesses. A small manufacturer should not have to wonder whether giving two customers different custom quotes could be considered "personalized pricing" simply because the resulting prices differ.

If a price varies because of who the customer is, based on personal data and estimated willingness to pay, transparency protections are appropriate. If it varies because the product, quantity, materials, labor, production requirements or contractual terms differ, it should be clearly recognized as ordinary customized pricing rather than personalized pricing.

New Jersey is now the third state to ban surveillance pricing by law. The FTC does not need to wait for all 50 states to act. It has the power to protect every American consumer now.

Ban surveillance pricing. Disclosure is not enough.

comment:
SUPPLEMENTAL COMMENT OF SIRVEIL, INC. - Docket FTC-2026-1057, Matter No. P034101

This supplements our comment of August 30, 2026 (FTC-2026-1057-0754). It adds new material only and does not repeat that comment.

DISCLOSURE OF INTEREST, FIRST. I run Sirveil, Inc., a two-person California company. We operate a service that answers one narrow question: for a named individual and a named public website, is that individual's information indexed there right now, with the source, the matching text and the time of retrieval. I have a commercial interest in this subject and disclose it here, as I did in August. Nothing below requires anyone to buy anything from my company; every step could be performed by Commission staff or any competent independent party.

THE SENTENCE THIS SUPPLEMENTAL ADDRESSES. The proposed statement says that "businesses that base personalized prices on personal data of consumers without sufficiently verifying that consumers consented to the collection of those data for that purpose may violate Section 5." Where the data were bought, "sufficiently verifying" is the whole question. Four developments the record may not yet reflect show what the available verification consists of.

1. California's deletion mechanism runs on the broker's own report. On August 25, 2026 the California Privacy Protection Agency reported half a million registered consumers, that "99.9% of consumers have already had their profile deleted by at least one broker," and that approximately 25% of the brokers in the system had reported processing requests. Every figure is broker-reported. The statute (Cal. Civ. Code 1798.99.86(b)(9)) gives a consumer the right to "verify the status" of a deletion request; the status shown is the status the broker entered. A business that verifies a consumer's consent by asking its data supplier is asking the same party that supplied the data.

2. Brokers' answers about deletion are not reliable on their face. A July 2026 preprint from UC Irvine (arXiv:2607.04552) sent deletion requests for synthetic identities that never existed; some brokers reported the data "deleted" (2.5% in the paper's Table 5), and only 97 of 322 brokers contacted reported any result at all. A peer-reviewed study that sent CCPA requests to all 543 California-registered brokers (IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, May 2026) found that "Above 40% failed to respond at all."

3. States are beginning to require traceability, not just deletion. Delaware HB 380 (85 Del. Laws c. 463, signed September 2, 2026, effective January 1, 2027) requires a controller that supplied a report used in a significant decision to identify, on request, "all third parties who obtained a report concerning the resident within the previous 24-months." The Commission's own Kochava order (entered June 25, 2026) likewise lets consumers "request the identity of any Recipient." Knowing where data went is now in the toolbox; knowing whether it is still there is the missing complement.

4. Congress may write the closed loop into statute. H.R. 8413 would deem a controller in compliance with a deletion request by "retaining a record of the deletion request and the minimum data necessary ... remains deleted." If enacted, the Commission would administer a regime in which deletion is complete on the respondent's own record. The statement should not assume a supplier's certificate of deletion means the data is gone.

PROPOSED LANGUAGE. I ask the Commission to add, after the sentence quoted above:

"For personal data obtained from a source other than the consumer, a business does not sufficiently verify consent by relying solely on the representations of the source or on its own records. Sufficient verification includes (1) identifying the source from which each data element used for pricing was obtained; (2) obtaining and retaining a dated representation from that source that the data are not subject to a deletion or opt-out request by the consumer; and (3) where the source is publicly accessible, retaining dated observation, not generated by the source, of whether the consumer's information remained available there at the time of use."

Three limits. This names no technology and no vendor; a Commission investigator or an auditor can perform each step. Observation of a public source shows what was available at a moment from a named source and nothing more; it cannot show what is inside anyone's systems. An indeterminate result must be recorded as indeterminate: a standard that rewards clean negatives will get clean negatives.

Respectfully submitted,
Ben Tobin, Founder and Chief Executive Officer, Sirveil, Inc., San Jose, California

Not legal advice: I write as a commercial party with a disclosed interest, not as counsel. Citations are as published; please confirm them against your own sources.

The proposed statement says that "businesses that base personalized prices on personal data of consumers without sufficiently verifying that consumers consented to the collection of those data for that purpose may violate Section 5." Where the data were bought, "sufficiently verifying" is the whole question. Four developments the record may not yet reflect show what the available verification consists of.

1. California's deletion mechanism runs on the broker's own report. On August 25, 2026 the California Privacy Protection Agency reported half a million registered consumers, that "99.9% of consumers have already had their profile deleted by at least one broker," and that approximately 25% of the brokers in the system had reported processing requests. Every figure is broker-reported. The statute (Cal. Civ. Code 1798.99.86(b)(9)) gives a consumer the right to "verify the status" of a deletion request; the status shown is the status the broker entered. A business that verifies a consumer's consent by asking its data supplier is asking the same party that supplied the data.

2. Brokers' answers about deletion are not reliable on their face. A July 2026 preprint from UC Irvine (arXiv:2607.04552) sent deletion requests for synthetic identities that never existed; some brokers reported the data "deleted" (2.5% in the paper's Table 5), and only 97 of 322 brokers contacted reported any result at all. A peer-reviewed study that sent CCPA requests to all 543 California-registered brokers (IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, May 2026) found that "Above 40% failed to respond at all."

3. States are beginning to require traceability, not just deletion. Delaware HB 380 (85 Del. Laws c. 463, signed September 2, 2026, effective January 1, 2027) requires a controller that supplied a report used in a significant decision to identify, on request, "all third parties who obtained a report concerning the resident within the previous 24-months." The Commission's own Kochava order (entered June 25, 2026) likewise lets consumers "request the identity of any Recipient." Knowing where data went is now in the toolbox; knowing whether it is still there is the missing complement.

4. Congress may write the closed loop into statute. H.R. 8413 would deem a controller in compliance with a deletion request by "retaining a record of the deletion request and the minimum data necessary ... remains deleted." If enacted, the Commission would administer a regime in which deletion is complete on the respondent's own record. The statement should not assume a supplier's certificate of deletion means the data is gone.

PROPOSED LANGUAGE. I ask the Commission to add, after the sentence quoted above:

"For personal data obtained from a source other than the consumer, a business does not sufficiently verify consent by relying solely on the representations of the source or on its own records. Three limits. This names no technology and no vendor; a Commission investigator or an auditor can perform each step. Observation of a public source shows what was available at a moment from a named source and nothing more; it cannot show what is inside anyone's systems. An indeterminate result must be recorded as indeterminate: a standard that rewards clean negatives will get clean negatives.

Respectfully submitted,
Ben Tobin, Founder and Chief Executive Officer, Sirveil, Inc., San Jose, California

comment:
The Center for Modern Commerce Policy is a nonpartisan nonprofit working on the policy barriers facing digital and omni-channel small businesses. I am writing as its Founder and Executive Director, and as a small business owner. For fourteen years I have run Sarah Wells Bags out of Fairfax, Virginia, making bags and apparel for new mothers. Our full comment is attached.

The Proposed Statement does not discuss discounts, and every example in it is a price that goes up. But personalization runs in two directions. If a discount to one customer counts as a personalized price, then every customer who did not receive it is paying more than the customer who did, for a reason the business knows about them. The disclosure obligation could land on the customers who are not getting the deal.

We offer a military discount. Under a plain reading, that could require a pop-up telling every customer who has not served that her price is higher because of it. We would not put that in front of our customers. We would stop offering the discount, and the service members it was built for would lose it. And if the discount disappears, the customer who did not serve is not better off. She pays exactly what she was paying before.

Conditional discounts have been ordinary in American retail for generations: grocery member pricing, senior and student discounts, birthday coupons, first-time customer offers. New York has already been through this. Its Algorithmic Pricing Disclosure Act said nothing about ordinary promotions, and the legislature has since passed the One Fair Price Act, writing in express protections for loyalty programs, coupons, and discounts for veterans, seniors, and teachers.

We ask the Commission to say plainly that ordinary conditional discounts are outside this statement, to give examples of what does not raise a concern, to clarify what form a disclosure must take, and to work with the Small Business Administration to get plain-language guidance in front of the owners who need it.

The Electronic Privacy Information Center (EPIC) and the undersigned organizations submit these comments in response to the Federal Trade Commission’s (FTC or Commission) Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement Regarding Personalized Pricing (Statement).

EPIC is an independent, nonpartisan public interest research center in Washington, D.C., established in 1994 to protect privacy, freedom of expression, and democratic values in the information age. For decades, EPIC has worked under different administrations to safeguard individuals’ personal data and to protect consumer privacy. EPIC focuses public attention on emerging consumer privacy issues, including the use of consumers’ personal information in ways that consumers do not expect and that harm them through things such as unfair or discriminatory pricing practices.

In February 2026, EPIC, along with fourteen other consumer groups, wrote a letter to the FTC, recommending that the FTC promulgate rules requiring companies to disclose the use of surveillance pricing technology. EPIC commends the Commission for taking action on this issue and agrees that consumers deserve to know when a price has been determined using their personal information. The FTC’s Statement outlines a comprehensive disclosure, one that will give consumers meaningful information about the types of data being used to set prices. However, based on both extensive expertise in limiting privacy harms and specific policy developments over the past year, EPIC believes that disclosure alone is not enough to adequately protect consumers from surveillance pricing in many instances. The Commission should clarify in its proposed enforcement policy statement that even many disclosed instances of surveillance pricing constitute an unfair practice, and it should consider using its Section 18 authority to promulgate a rule banning the practice.

A growing body of consumer polling, state legislative action, and the FTC’s own past actions on unfair data practices all point to the same conclusion: surveillance pricing causes substantial, unavoidable consumer harm that transparency alone cannot cure. The Commission should not lag behind a regulatory landscape that has moved decisively in this direction. States and localities, consumers, and advocacy groups like EPIC are deeply concerned about the affordability and privacy harms of surveillance pricing that cannot be fully ameliorated by transparency. The FTC should be too.

EPIC recommends that the Commission update its Proposed Enforcement Policy to reflect that surveillance pricing constitutes an unfair practice under Section 5 of the FTC Act, and use its rulemaking and enforcement authority to prohibit surveillance pricing practices that cause substantial, unavoidable consumer harm rather than limit its response to disclosure-based remedies.

The International Center for Law & Economics (ICLE) respectfully submits these comments regarding the Commission’s Proposed Enforcement Policy Statement on Personalized Pricing. While we support transparent, competitive markets, we urge the Commission to withdraw or substantially revise the Proposed Statement.

The proposal treats the non-disclosure of personalized pricing as presumptively unfair or deceptive under Section 5. Yet the Commission explicitly concedes that the practice's real-world prevalence is unknown and its effects on consumers are “unclear”. Converting empirical uncertainty into presumptive liability violates Section 5(n) and risks deterring pro-consumer discounting.

Our detailed comments highlight several core legal and economic deficiencies:

UNSUBSTANTIATED ECONOMIC CLAIMS: The assertion that greater pricing sophistication reduces consumer benefit is unsupported by the cited literature. Across the empirical studies cited, personalized pricing lowers prices for the majority of buyers and expands market output. Where consumer harm arises, it stems from market power or asymmetric data access—not data granularity per se.

DEFICIENT UNFAIRNESS ANALYSIS: Under Section 5(n) and FTC v. Corpay, Inc., unfairness requires substantial consumer injury that is not reasonably avoidable and not outweighed by countervailing benefits. The Commission skips this mandatory balancing across its hypothetical examples and improperly leans on subjective perceptions of fairness.

FLAWED DECEPTION THEORY: A displayed price indicates the terms of purchase; it does not affirmatively promise uniform treatment across all buyers. Under International Harvester, pure omissions absent an affirmative misleading claim cannot establish deception.

PERVERSE REGULATORY INCENTIVES: Mandating complex algorithmic and data-source disclosures will induce information overload and trigger a “hydraulic effect,” encouraging retailers to abandon beneficial targeted discounts in favor of rigid, higher uniform prices.

If the Commission proceeds, it should: (1) withdraw the sophistication claim; (2) clarify that displayed prices do not imply uniformity; (3) ground deception strictly in express or implied representations; (4) establish a clear safe harbor for general variation notices; (5) expressly exclude loyalty discounts and coupons from presumptive illegality; and (6) rigorously apply Section 5(n)’s mandatory balancing test to its enforcement examples.
